segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now concerning the matters you wrote about:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But because of cases of sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife, and each woman should have her own husband.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The husband should give his wife what is owed to her, and likewise the wife to her husband.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; and likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer and then be together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I say this as a concession, not as a command.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I wish that all people were as I myself am. But each has their own gift from God, one of one kind and another of another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them if they remain as I also am.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if they are not exercising self-control, they should marry, for it is better to marry than to burn.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To the married I give this charge—not I, but the Lord—that a wife must not separate from her husband;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but if she does separate, she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband—and that a husband must not divorce his wife.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To the rest I say—I, not the Lord—that if any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, he must not divorce her.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if any woman has an unbelieving husband and he consents to live with her, she must not divorce her husband.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the unbelieving husband has been made holy through his wife, and the unbelieving wife has been made holy through the brother. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is they are holy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if the unbeliever separates, let him separate. The brother or the sister is not enslaved in such cases; God has called us to peace.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Only, let each one walk as the Lord has apportioned to each, as God has called each. This is what I direct in all the assemblies.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Was anyone called when already circumcised? He should not reverse his circumcision. Has anyone been called while uncircumcised? He should not be circumcised.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing; what matters is keeping God’s commandments.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Each person should remain in the calling in which they were called.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Were you called as a slave? Do not let it trouble you. But if you can in fact become free, by all means take the opportunity.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the one who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freed person; likewise the one who was called as a free person is Christ’s slave.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Brothers and sisters, each one should remain with God in the condition in which they were called.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now concerning the virgins, I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is faithful.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I think, then, that this is good in view of the present distress: that it is good for a person to remain just as they are.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if you do marry, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. Yet such people will have affliction in the flesh, and I am trying to spare you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What I mean is this, brothers and sisters: the time has been cut short. From now on, even those who have wives should be as though they had none,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: those who weep as though they were not weeping, those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, those who buy as though they owned nothing,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and those who make use of the world as though they were not making full use of it. For the form of this world is passing away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I want you to be free from concern. The unmarried man is concerned about the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the married man is concerned about the things of the world, how he may please his wife,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he is divided. Both the unmarried woman and the virgin are concerned about the things of the Lord, so as to be holy in both body and spirit. But the married woman is concerned about the things of the world, how she may please her husband.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I say this for your own benefit, not to throw a noose over you, but to promote what is proper and undistracted devotion to the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if anyone thinks he is behaving improperly toward his betrothed, if his passions are strong and so it has to be, let him do what he wishes; he is not sinning. Let them marry.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the one who stands firm in his heart, who is under no compulsion but has authority over his own will, and has decided in his own heart to keep his betrothed as she is, will do well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the one who marries his betrothed does well, and the one who does not marry will do better.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A wife is bound for as long as her husband lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whomever she wishes, only in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But in my judgment she is more blessed if she remains as she is—and I think that I too have the Spirit of God.

notes.phrase: It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman
notes.note: Greek manuscripts have no quotation marks. Most recent scholars take this sentence as a statement from the Corinthians’ letter, which Paul quotes and then qualifies in the verses that follow. The older view reads it as Paul’s own opinion. The text follows the first view and marks the sentence as a quotation.

The Greek says “to touch a woman,” an established euphemism for sexual intercourse, found also in the Septuagint (for example Genesis 20:6). A modern reader could take “touch” to mean any physical contact, so the sense is given directly. Several recent translations do the same.

The Greek has only the verb “to burn.” Most interpreters understand it as burning with sexual desire, which fits the mention of self-control, and many translations add “with passion.” A minority take it as burning in judgment.

Paul is referring to a teaching of Jesus on divorce, of the kind preserved in the Gospels (for example Mark 10:2–12). In verse 12 he has no such saying to cite and gives his own instruction. The two verbs here, “separate” and “divorce,” were both used for ending a marriage; the ancient world did not distinguish legal separation from divorce.

The Greek verb is built on the ordinary word for “holy,” the same word used of the children at the end of the verse; “made holy” keeps that link visible where the traditional “sanctified” hides it. Paul does not mean the unbelieving spouse is saved (see verse 16). The point seems to be that the marriage does not defile the believer but brings the family within the sphere of what belongs to God, though the exact sense is debated.

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the one Greek word is recognizable.

The verb refers to a known procedure by which some Jewish men sought to restore the appearance of a foreskin, usually to avoid ridicule when exercising naked in Greek society. 1 Maccabees 1:15 mentions the practice.

notes.phrase: by all means take the opportunity
notes.note: The Greek says only “rather make use,” with no object. Most modern interpreters supply “freedom”: a slave who can gain freedom should take it. Many ancient and some modern interpreters supply “slavery”: even if you can become free, make the most of your present condition. The grammar allows both, and the text follows the majority view.

The participle can mean “present” or “impending,” so some translations have “the impending crisis.” It is also disputed whether Paul means a local hardship in Corinth, the general pressures on believers, or the troubles expected before the end (compare verses 29–31).

The Greek word is an ordinary term for hardship that presses on a person. This translation renders it “affliction” throughout, so that the reader can see the same word wherever it occurs. Most versions here have “trouble” or “distress.”

notes.traditional: There is difference also between a wife and a virgin
notes.note: The manuscripts differ in wording and punctuation across verses 33–34. One form of the text, followed by the King James Version, begins a new sentence here: “There is a difference also between the wife and the virgin.” The reading translated here, in which the married man is “divided,” is the one adopted in modern critical editions.

The Greek says literally “his virgin.” The text follows most recent translations in taking verses 36–38 to address a man and the woman he is engaged to. The older view, still defended, is that Paul addresses a father deciding whether to give his daughter in marriage; in its favor, the verb in verse 38 normally means “give in marriage” rather than “marry.” The choice affects the rendering of all three verses.

notes.traditional: if she pass the flower of her age
notes.note: The Greek adjective is rare, and the verb has no expressed subject. It may describe the woman as past the usual age for marriage, or the man as having strong sexual desire. The text takes the second, which fits the contrast with the man in verse 37 who is under no compulsion, but the evidence does not settle the question.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the Gospels, Acts, Paul and Revelation, and versions vary between “fornication,” “sexual immorality,” “prostitution” and “unchastity,” which obscures that it is one word.
The plural address occurs throughout the letters, and the choice between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters” needs to be uniform across all chapters.
Translations vary between “slave,” “servant” and “bondservant,” and the choice affects both literal slavery passages and the metaphor of being Christ’s slave.
The figurative use for conduct is frequent in Paul and John, and translators split between keeping the Semitic idiom “walk” and rendering it “live.”
The sleep euphemism for death recurs (1 Corinthians 11 and 15, 1 Thessalonians 4, John 11, Acts 7) and a single policy is needed on whether to keep “fall asleep” or translate as “die.”
